title: US tariff response plan and Bill 17 stance
subtitle: Six Nations training, noise by-law overhaul, heritage designations, Dearborn service centre funding, and a Herb Street apartment proposal.
overview: Council approved a 10-point response to US tariffs {{vote:m4}}. It includes a procurement by-law change to favour Canadian businesses, an optional tax deferral for industrial and commercial property owners, a Buy Waterloo campaign, and a request that the economic development advisory committee develop a MedTech accelerator initiative.

Council also approved a new Noise By-Law with a tiered exemption system and lower fees for community events {{vote:m6}}. It moved funding to expand the Dearborn service centre {{vote:m8}} and designated two properties as heritage sites while withdrawing notices on three others {{vote:m9}}. On provincial legislation, council voted to oppose parts of Bill 5 {{vote:m11}} and to advocate against Bill 17 limits on local green building standards {{vote:m12}}. It endorsed the Age-friendly Action Plan 2025-2026 {{vote:m5}} and amended the Parkade agreement with the Region {{vote:m3}}.

The afternoon included an education session with Six Nations representatives on treaty rights and the duty to consult. In the evening, council held an informal public meeting on an eight-storey rental building proposed for Erb Street West. No decision was made, and staff will report back later.

decisions.detail: Council approved the 10-point plan, including procurement by-law changes favouring Canadian businesses, a tax deferral program, a Buy Waterloo campaign and a MedTech accelerator request to the advisory committee.
Council approved a revised Noise By-Law with a new exemption process, reduced exemption fees and related penalty and fee by-law amendments.
Council released and reallocated $232,000 for 2025 and advanced $1.768 million from 2026 from the West Side Satellite Operations Centre project to the Dearborn Service Centre expansion.
Council designated 75 Allen Street East and 39 Dupont Street East under the Ontario Heritage Act and withdrew notices of intention to designate for three other properties.
Council accepted the Sustainability Advisory Committee report and directed staff and elected officials to oppose Bill 5 provisions that would erode municipal planning authority.

Council resolved to advocate removing Bill 17 limits on local planning authority over High-Performance Development Standards, to comment through the Environmental Registry, and to continue developing local standards.
Council endorsed the Age-friendly Action Plan 2025-2026 and approved the related report.
Council authorized the Mayor and Clerk to sign an amendment to the 2023 Option and Governance Agreement with the Region relating to the Parkade.

debate: On the tariff plan, councillors asked about timelines, whether Canadian-labelled goods could cost more, and whether demand for Canadian suppliers could strain them. Staff said procurement weighs value and not only price, and that about 96% of city spending already goes to Canadian suppliers. A delegate asked for equity and inclusion criteria in procurement. Staff pointed to the existing social procurement policy, and the Mayor suggested the advisory committee consider it.

On the Noise By-Law, one councillor raised concern that construction noise at night, including vibration, has no clear tool, and asked how bad actors are handled. Staff said exemptions can be revoked, orders issued and daily charges laid. A delegate argued for tighter exemptions tied to compliance with all city by-laws and stronger enforcement.

On the Herb Street West proposal, residents raised concerns about height, traffic on Coulter-type local streets, parking overflow, demolition of existing affordable units, and construction impacts. Councillors asked staff to widen the traffic study and coordinate with the Region on access. The applicant's planners cited a 10% affordable component and a right of first refusal for current tenants.

On Bill 5 and Bill 17, councillors and delegates argued that rolling back environmental protections and local standards would raise long-term energy, water and retrofit costs and weaken treaty consultation. Delegates said high-performance standards need not slow housing starts.

Six Nations representatives said consultation is unclear, that provincial bills tend to weaken it, and asked for a dedicated municipal team and a clear protocol. Staff said a region-wide consultation protocol is close to finished.
